a: Capturing data as it travels across a network
Encrypting data before it is sent
Deleting data from a server
Flooding a network with traffic
tasks.fb: The data still arrives, so the victim may never know.

tasks.q: Which is an example of data theft rather than interception?
a: A laptop full of customer records is stolen from a car
Packets are captured on public Wi-Fi
A router is monitored by software
Traffic is copied as it crosses a switch
tasks.fb: Theft takes the data at rest; interception takes it in transit.

tasks.q: What does packet sniffer software do?
a: Captures and examines the packets travelling across a network
Blocks websites for children
Encrypts a hard drive
Backs up files automatically
tasks.fb: It's a normal network management tool that attackers misuse.

tasks.q: Why is free public Wi-Fi risky?
a: Traffic may be unencrypted, and anyone nearby could capture it
It is always slower
It uses more battery
It cannot reach secure websites
tasks.fb: Attackers also set up fake hotspots with convincing names.

tasks.q: In a man-in-the-middle attack, what does the attacker do?
a: Sits between the two parties, reading and passing on the messages
Blocks all traffic to the website
Encrypts the victim's files
Guesses passwords repeatedly
tasks.fb: Neither side realises anyone is in between.

tasks.q: Which warning sign might suggest a fake hotspot?
a: An open network with a convincing name and no password
A network that asks for WPA2 security
A network with a padlock icon
A network named after your own router
tasks.fb: Open networks give attackers the easiest route in.

tasks.q: Why is intercepted data valuable to criminals?
a: It can be used for fraud, or sold to others
It makes their internet faster
It proves their software works
It deletes their own records
tasks.fb: Stolen data is traded openly on criminal marketplaces.

tasks.q: Which everyday habit most increases the risk of data theft?
a: Writing passwords down and leaving them by the computer
Locking your screen
Using a password manager
Updating your phone
tasks.fb: People remain the easiest way in.

tasks.q: How does encryption protect data in transit?
a: Intercepted data can't be understood without the key
It stops packets being captured at all
It makes the network faster
It deletes the attacker's copy
tasks.fb: You can't stop someone capturing packets, but you can make them worthless.

a: Encrypts all your traffic between your device and a trusted server
Blocks adverts only
Speeds up your broadband
Stops your device needing a password
tasks.fb: That's why VPNs are recommended on public Wi-Fi.

tasks.q: Which of these reduce the risk of data interception and theft? Select all that apply.
opts: Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi
Sharing one login for the whole office
Keeping the server room door propped open
correct: Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi
tasks.fb: The last two create exactly the weaknesses attackers look for.

tasks.q: Is each habit safe or risky?
items: Banking on open café Wi-Fi with no VPN
Checking the padlock and HTTPS before logging in
Leaving a laptop unlocked at a desk
Writing the Wi-Fi password on the office whiteboard
Using a VPN when working away from the office
Emailing a spreadsheet of personal data unencrypted
tasks.fb: Most of the risky ones are about people, not technology.

info.title: Wireshark
info.text: Wireshark is a free packet sniffer used by network managers worldwide. The same tool in the wrong hands is an attacker's dream.

info.title: HTTPS everywhere
info.text: Most websites now use HTTPS by default, which is why intercepting browsing is far less useful than it once was.

info.title: Evil twin
info.text: A fake hotspot with the same name as a real one is called an evil twin. Phones may join it automatically.

info.title: Data protection law
info.text: UK law requires organisations to protect personal data. Serious breaches can lead to very large fines.

info.title: Shoulder to shoulder
info.text: Interception isn't always technical: reading a screen on a train, or a document on a printer, works too.

info.title: Encrypted devices
info.text: Modern phones and laptops encrypt their storage, so a stolen device doesn't hand over its data.
